The link: between a node (a task, and as well a decision, lesson or finding) and a doc's path in the project (docs/guide/setup.md). Made and removed through the log like every other change (doc.link and doc.unlink, by whoever did it, in the node's history and the Activity feed); any number each way.
- In the app, the detail panel gains a Docs section: the node's docs (named by their first heading, the path under it), a click opening the doc in the Docs view, × to unlink, and Link a doc… (the palette, picking among the docs).
- The Docs view shows, under the open doc, the nodes linked to it (key, state, title), a click opening one in the detail panel, × to unlink, and Link a task… (the palette, picking among the nodes).
- On the command line, for Claude and scripts: livtk doc link KEY PATH, livtk doc unlink KEY PATH, livtk doc links KEY (a node's docs) and livtk doc links PATH (a doc's nodes); livtk show lists a node's docs.
- A doc moved or deleted keeps its links, shown as missing (its path, struck), to unlink or to link again where it went.
Unchanged from the plan above: where Docs sits, the tree, the rendering, links inside docs, the palette's Open doc.
Tests, added: linking and unlinking from either end and through the CLI, many to many, each in the history; a missing doc's links; the detail panel's and the view's lists.

Built: Docs in the Views group (g o, the rail, the View menu): the project's markdown under docs/ (or config.toml's docs = "...") as a tree (folders first and shut or open, README/index first, docs named by their first heading; J/K/Enter) and the open doc in the app's markdown at a reading width, remembered per project; read again when files change on disk. Links in docs: another doc (relative, ../, /, #anchor) opens here, a bare key (TAS-12, not in code) opens the node in the panel, the web in the browser. Docs and nodes linked many to many through the log (doc.link / doc.unlink, format 4; signals doc.linked / doc.unlinked): under the doc, its nodes (open, unlink, Link a task…); in the panel, a node's docs (open, unlink, missing struck) and Add link → A doc…; the palette finds and opens docs. CLI: livtk doc list | link | unlink | links, and docs in livtk show. Not yet: editing, images, diagrams, search inside docs.

Review: a rebuild from the log clears doc links too (a checkout that drops a link takes it away); the CLI reads doc paths from the folder it runs in; keys in link text, URLs, autolinks, indented code and reference definitions stay unlinked; links percent-decoded, queries dropped; titles keep their own #; a remembered doc gone gives way to the first; the refresh check skips hidden files and watches the open doc wherever it is; an absolute path through a linked folder still finds the project.

data.title: Docs: the reader as a product, and the app's feel
data.body:
The docs work, but they read like a file viewer, not a product. This task makes them one, and with them the app's feel overall. Agreed in chat (2026-10-18): all of it.

Icons
- The tree is noisy: every doc row carries the same book icon, folders only a tiny caret. A doc gets a light glyph (article) or none, folders their folder / folder-open icons.
- Terminal (chevrons) and Docs (book-content) were stand-ins. One consistent icon pass across the sidebar, the tree, the palette and the panel, from the set now in assets (terminal, book, article, folder-open, hashtag, list, copy-list, ...).

The reader
1. Reading typography: a reading size (15-16px), line height about 1.65, a real heading scale and spacing, about 70 characters a line; code blocks with a copy button; tables and quotes styled.
2. A real doc header: the first heading promoted as the title, a breadcrumb (Docs > Guide > Setup), when it last changed, and the linked tasks at the top as state-coloured chips, not buried at the bottom.
3. "On this page": a slim right rail of the headings, scroll-spy highlighting where you are, a click jumping there; #anchor links actually land.
4. Navigation: back and forward (Cmd-[ / Cmd-]), previous and next doc at the bottom, Cmd-F to find in the page.
5. Search across docs: full text, results with highlighted snippets, from the palette and the tree.
6. Richer markdown: callouts (> [!NOTE], > [!WARNING], as GitHub draws them), local images, mermaid diagrams, frontmatter (title, status, tags).
7. Backlinks: "Mentioned in", the tasks and docs that mention or link to this doc, so docs feel connected rather than filed away.
8. Editing: "Open in editor" ($EDITOR / VS Code) first, then inline editing.

The product overall
- Claude uses docs: when Claude starts a task, its linked docs are put in front of it (the session hook lists them), so links are working context, not bookkeeping.
- First run: an empty project offers to create docs/ with a starter README; empty states with an action, not only text.
- One quiet motion language: a subtle fade as the doc changes, smooth scroll to anchors, as the panel and the bottom bar slide.
- Settings: reading font size and density; later a light theme.
- A consistency audit: icon sizes, hovers, menus and spacing, one pass across every view, so it feels made by one hand.

data.text:
Plan (Claude), 2026-10-18. For the developer's ack. Built in phases, each committed and installed as it lands, so each can be looked at live.
A. Icons and the reader's frame: the icon pass (Terminal: terminal; Docs: book; a doc: article; folders: folder / folder-open; the outline: list; headings: hashtag), the reading typography (16px, 1.65 line height, a heading scale, ~70 characters a line, code with a copy button, tables and quotes styled), the doc header (title, breadcrumb, last changed, linked tasks as chips at the top), On this page with scroll-spy and anchors that land, back and forward (Cmd-[ / Cmd-]), previous and next doc, Cmd-F to find in the page.
B. Connected docs: search across docs (full text, snippets, from the palette and the tree's filter), backlinks (Mentioned in: tasks and docs that mention or link to the doc).
C. Richer markdown: callouts (> [!NOTE] / [!TIP] / [!IMPORTANT] / [!WARNING] / [!CAUTION]), local images, frontmatter (title, status, tags), mermaid diagrams drawn in-app by mermaid-rs-renderer (pure Rust, to SVG; no browser).
D. Editing: Open in editor ($EDITOR, else VS Code, else the system's), then inline editing: Edit on the doc swaps the reader for the markdown, Cmd-S saves, Esc leaves, a change on disk meanwhile asks before overwriting.
E. Claude uses docs: livtk start / show and the session hook put a task's linked docs in front of Claude (their paths and titles, to read).
F. The feel: first run (an empty project offers docs/ with a starter README; empty states get an action), one quiet motion language (a fade as the doc changes, smooth scroll to anchors), settings (reading size and density; the light theme stays later, as said), and a consistency audit across every view.
Tests: the logic in each (outline from headings, anchors, history, find, search and snippets, backlinks, callouts and frontmatter parsed, the editor's save and conflict, what the hook says); the look is judged live.

Phase A built: icons (Docs: book; folders: folder / folder-open; no icon on every doc; the outline: list; copy); the reader as a column of sections at the headings, at 16px and 1.65 line height, ~70 characters a line, a heading scale, code blocks with a copy button; a header (Docs › folders, the title, when it was edited, the path, the linked tasks as chips with × and Link a task); On this page (the headings, the one being read lit, a click going there); doc.md#heading links land on it; previous and next doc at the bottom; Cmd-[ / Cmd-] back and forward; Cmd-F a find bar (matches highlighted, Enter / Shift-Enter between them, Esc shuts it), kept outside the list's keys so typing in it is text.

Phase B built: a search at the tree's top (outside the list's keys): titles first, then text, each doc with the lines it is in; a result opens with the find bar on the query; Enter opens the first. The palette finds docs by their text too, with the line. Under each doc, Mentioned in: the docs linking to it (relative, root and reference links, autolinks) and the tasks whose title, plan or notes name its path without being linked.

Phase C built: callouts (> [!NOTE] / [!TIP] / [!IMPORTANT] / [!WARNING] / [!CAUTION], an optional title after the marker) as boxes with a bar and icon in their colour; mermaid fences drawn in-app by mermaid-rs-renderer to SVG in a theme of the app's dark, cached per diagram, narrowed to the doc's width, a broken one showing why; local images loaded from the doc's own folder; frontmatter (title, status, tags) read off the top: the title over the heading's, the status and #tags in the header.

Phase D built: in the doc's header, Edit and Open in editor ($VISUAL, else VS Code, else the system's text editor). Edit puts the doc's markdown in the reader's place (outside the list's keys), a dot while unsaved; Cmd-S writes it, refusing to write over a file changed on disk meanwhile (Save over it / Take theirs); Esc leaves, asking first while unsaved (Discard / Save and close); opening another doc ends the edit.

Phase E built: livtk start names the docs a task is linked to (read: path  title); the session's brief lists them under each task in progress (docs to read: ...); the work skill and the implementer read them, and update a doc a change alters.

Phase F built: empty states with a way on (Open a project, New task, Clear the filter, Start the docs: a README in docs/); a doc fades in and the reader glides to a heading (still, with Reduce Motion); Settings (Cmd-comma, the app menu): the docs' text size (small, regular, large) and density (comfortable, compact), kept. A consistency pass: the docs' and the grid's buttons, rows, fields and chips on the app's radii, sizes and hovers; icon buttons with hover-lit icons and tooltips (the find bar, copy, unlink on a doc's chips, a toast's close); section labels all medium; chips 20 high and full-round; the editor's bar 46 high as the other headers; the update row as the sidebar's rows. Left as they are: the graph's accent ring on the chosen card (a spatial view's focus); list density beyond the reader.

data.title: Docs in the app's grammar: list, reader, panel
data.body:
The docs view builds its own small site inside the middle pane (a tree with its own border and rounded sidebar-style rows, a floating search field, an outline column, a web-page header), so it does not match tasks or the terminal. Rebuild it from the app's grammar (docs/design.md): a list in the middle, open one, its details in the panel. Agreed in chat (2026-10-18).

The list (middle)
- The docs as list rows like tasks: 36px, full width, hairlines, the gliding highlight, J / K / Enter.
- Folders as the task list's group bands (collapsible, with a count); nested folders named by their path (Guide / Setup).
- Each row: a doc slot, the title, the linked tasks' state marks, edited time on the right.
- Search through the top filter, not a field of its own; results as rows with the matched line.

The reader (middle, in the list's place)
- Opening a doc takes the list's place, as the terminal does, behind a 46px header bar: back / forward, the path as crumbs, Edit, Open in editor, close. Esc gives the list back.
- Below the bar only the doc: title and text, the same measure and typography. Find, mermaid, callouts, images, the editor stay.

The panel (right)
- The doc's details laid out as a task's: properties (status, tags, edited, path), linked tasks as live rows with their states (linking as "Add link" does on a task), Mentioned in, and On this page (the outline, following the scroll).

Gone: the inner tree column, the floating search field, the outline column, the in-page header and chips.

data.text: Plan (Claude), 2026-10-18. For the developer's ack. Phases, each installed and committed as it lands. A: the list: docs as rows and folder bands in the middle (the tree's model kept underneath: rows from it, collapsing as now), the inner column and floating field removed, search moved into the filter. B: the reader in the list's place behind a 46px bar (as the terminal is placed), Esc and close back to the list, back/forward and crumbs in the bar; the in-page header reduced to the title. C: the panel: a doc detail beside the task detail (properties, linked tasks as rows with state buttons, Add link through the existing picker, Mentioned in, On this page with scroll-spy); the outline column and chips removed. Tests: model tests for rows/bands and open/close; app tests for keys (J/K/Enter/Esc), the reader taking the list's place, the panel's links and outline jumps. Grammar written to docs/design.md.

Built: the docs as a list in the middle (36px rows, folder bands with counts, folded with their subfolders; each doc with its linked tasks' state marks and when it was edited; J/K glide, Enter reads, a click reads), search through the dock's filter (found docs as rows with their line; opening one puts the find bar on the query). A doc read takes the list's place behind a 46px bar (back, forward, Docs > folders > title crumbs, Edit, Open in editor, close); J/K scroll it; Esc and close give the list back on the doc. Its details in the panel, as a task's: Status, Tags, Edited, Path; Tasks (linked, a click opens the task in the panel, Esc gives the doc's details back; Link a task); Mentioned in; On this page following the scroll. The panel's close and the panel key put it away and bring it back. Gone: the tree column, the floating search field, the outline column, the in-page crumbs and chips. Order everywhere (first doc, previous/next) is the list's: top-level docs, then each folder's. Tests: model (bands, folding, reading, marks, search rows, neighbours) and UI (list keys, reader in the list's place, panel, Esc order, filter search). 227 app tests; full check passes.

review: REFUTED. (1) Closing the reader with its bar's close or the Docs crumb (ui/docs.rs:453,520 -> leave_doc) leaves reader.finding set, so after opening a doc from a filter search the find bar stays floating over the list (ui/mod.rs:6265); probe confirmed. (2) Deleting the doc being read: load_docs falls back to the first doc with reading still true (model/docs.rs:466-472), so the reader silently swaps to a different doc instead of giving the list back; probe confirmed. (3) The top bar's panel toggle still lights on model.detail only (ui/mod.rs:2573), so it shows off while the doc panel is open. (4) J from a folder band down onto a doc: spot() counts bands (ui/mod.rs:1444) so a glide starts, but doc_band draws no glide, so the highlight blinks out for the glide. (5) open_doc from a task's panel or the palette goes to Docs without sync_filter, so the filter field can hold the tasks' filter while docs.query differs. Esc order, panel width/edge/float, index clamping after fold/search/refresh, whitespace query and prev/next order hold. 24 docs tests pass.

Review fixes (all five REFUTED points): leaving the reader by its close or the Docs crumb shuts the find bar too; the doc being read gone from disk gives the list back rather than another doc; the top bar's panel button lights for the doc panel; a band draws the gliding highlight, so J from a band onto a doc never blinks; arriving at a view any way syncs the filter field to that view's (docs: the search). Regression tests for the first two; 228 app tests, full check passes.

data.title: Docs list nests: folders as a tree in the list
data.body:
The docs list nests folders as a tree, still as the list (docs/design.md), not a sidebar. Agreed in chat (2026-10-18).

- Rows: every line a full-width 36px list row, the gliding highlight. Folders are rows (caret, folder / folder-open, name, count) instead of bands; each level indents about 20px, with a 1px guide line under each open folder down to its last child. Docs keep their linked tasks' marks and edited time, aligned at the right whatever the depth.
- Keys: J / K move; Enter reads a doc or folds a folder; Right unfolds a folder or steps into it; Left folds it or goes to its parent. A click on a caret folds, on a doc reads.
- Folded folders remembered per project; opening a doc unfolds its folders. Fold all / unfold all in the dock beside Filter.
- Search lists what it found flat, each with its folder path dimmed; cleared, the tree again.
- Tests: rows with depth and last-child, keys (Left / Right, parents), folding remembered, search flat.

data.text: Plan (Claude), 2026-10-18. For the developer's ack. Model: DocRow::Folder { path, name, depth, count, open, last } and DocRow::Doc gains depth and last (rows() walks the tree: a folder's docs, then its folders? no: top-level docs first as now, then within each folder its docs then its subfolders, matching ordered()), plus the open ancestors' guide columns per row; shut folders saved in app state per project; fold_all / unfold_all; docs_left / docs_right. Keys: H/Left and L/Right already move between board columns (PrevColumn / NextColumn); in the Docs list they fold/parent and unfold/step in, so no new bindings. UI: one row component for folders and docs at their depth with guide lines drawn as 1px absolute divs; the band code goes. Dock: Fold all / Unfold all (chevrons-down-up). Search rows flat with the path dimmed. Tests: model (rows depth/last/guides, Left/Right, parents, fold-all, remembered across save/restore, search flat) and UI (arrow keys, caret click, glide unchanged).

Built: the docs list nests. Folders are list rows at their depth (caret, folder / folder-open, name, count), docs under them a level in (20px a level, a caret's slot kept so icons line up), a 1px guide down each folder's lines; the gliding highlight and right-aligned marks and edited time as before. Keys: Enter folds a folder or reads a doc; Right opens a shut folder, then steps in; Left shuts an open folder, else goes to its folder (the board's H/L and arrows, routed in the Docs view). Fold all in the dock (lit, Unfold all, once every folder is shut; shown when there are folders and no search). Folding keeps the highlight on its line, else on the shut folder holding it. Folds are kept per project and across restarts (app.toml docs_shut). Search lists flat, each doc with its folder dimmed. Tests: rows' depth and order, Left/Right/parents, fold all and its memory across save/restore, UI arrows and Fold all. 229 app tests; full check passes.

review: REFUTED x2. (1) show_doc (model/docs.rs:650-655) edits docs.shut and keep_shut()s it without loading the current project's folds first: switch project outside the Docs view (select_project only reloads docs in Docs), then open a doc (follow a link, palette) -> project A's folds overwrite project B's in docs_shut (probe: B had docs/other shut, ended with only A's docs/guide). Fix: take self.docs.shut from docs_shut[current] before removing ancestors. (2) select_column_by (model.rs:808) routes h/l/arrows to docs_left/right while a doc is being read: Left twice shuts the read doc's folder (persisted), leave_doc then lands on the folder. Guard with !docs.reading. Rest held: parent_row, prefix '/' handling, search flat, dock gating, ordering.

Review fixes (both REFUTED points): opening a doc from outside the view loads that project's folds first, so one project's folds never overwrite another's; while reading, Left / Right / H / L do nothing to the list. Regression test for both; 230 app tests, full check passes.

data.title: Panes: any view in any pane, split and placeholders
data.body:
The middle of the window becomes a layout of panes instead of one view: each pane shows any view (Tasks, Docs, Terminal, Graph, Activity, Inbox, ...) with its own state, panes split side by side or stacked, and an empty pane is a placeholder that offers the views to put in it. First use: the terminal on the left, tasks on the right. Agreed in chat (2026-10-19).

The grammar (docs/design.md changes first)
- Left: navigation, as now. It acts on the focused pane: a view picked there goes into it.
- Middle: a split of panes, each a view edge to edge with its own selection, scroll, filter and dock. One pane is focused: the keys, the sidebar and the dock are its. A thin divider between panes resizes them.
- Right: the panel stays what is open: the thing chosen in the focused pane (a task, a doc). So the terminal and a task list sit side by side, and a task opened from the list shows in the panel.
- A placeholder pane: an empty pane with the views to choose from (click, or its key). A split starts as one.

Doing
- Split right / split down / close pane / focus the next pane: palette commands and keys; a pane's bar has split and close on hover.
- Panes remember their layout, views and sizes per window across restarts.
- A terminal per pane (a second terminal pane is a second shell).

Built in phases, each installed and committed: A model: per-pane view state, one pane, no change in behaviour; B UI: the split, focus, dividers, keys; C placeholders; D memory, commands, terminals per pane; the grammar doc and tests along the way.

data.text: Plan (Claude), 2026-10-19. For the developer's ack. Model: a Pane holds what is now the view's state in Model (view, layout, rows, groups, filtered, selected, band, leaving, displays, collapsed, docs list/reading, graph camera, feed index); Model keeps panes: Vec<Pane>, a split tree (Split { axis, children with fractions } | Leaf(pane id)) and the focused pane, and shares the rest (projects, the panel's detail, palette, toasts, flashes, docs folds). Phase A moves state behind self.pane() with one pane and every test unchanged. UI: each pane renders its view with its own scroll handles and key context (keys reach only the focused pane, so the board/list/terminal key rules hold per pane); the panel follows the focused pane. Keys: split right / down, close pane, next pane (exact keys chosen against the current map). Saved: the tree, each pane's view and display, fractions. Terminals keyed by pane. Tests: model (split/close/focus, a view per pane with separate selection and filter, the panel following focus, restore) and UI (two panes side by side, keys going only to the focused one, the placeholder picking a view, terminal + tasks).

Phase A built: a Pane holds a view's own state (view, layout, rows, groups, filtered, selection, band, leaving, everything it holds, nesting depth, progress); the model keeps the panes, the one acted on (focused, or for a moment another through with_pane), and a Split tree (Pane(id) | Split { axis, parts with shares }). Each view shows in one pane at most: asking for a view another pane shows focuses that pane, so what a view keeps by itself (docs, graph, feed, displays) stays shared. Split (a focused placeholder beside, the same axis joining rather than nesting), close (room back to the rest, the one before focused, never the last), next pane. Every pane is brought up to date on a change. No change on screen yet: one pane. Model tests for splitting, closing, focus, per-pane selection, one pane per view, and updates reaching unfocused panes. 233 app tests; full check passes.

Changed with the developer (2026-10-19): no terminal per pane. Terminals go the VS Code way instead: the Terminal view holds several terminals (a list of them, + for a new one, kill, rename), in one pane like every view.

Phases B and C built: the middle draws the split, each pane in its own content box with a gutter between; the focused pane is drawn with the keys (list keys, terminal, doc editor), its dock and the docs' find bar; the others drawn as they stand, a press in one focuses it (and its terminal takes the keys). Dividers drag to move the room between panes. A placeholder pane offers every view (one shown elsewhere goes to its pane) and Close pane; the sidebar and the G keys fill it. Keys: Cmd-\ split right, Cmd-Alt-\ split down, Cmd-Alt-W close, Cmd-Alt-] / [ next and previous pane. The panel follows what the focused pane opens. Lists scroll per pane; the bottom bar spans every pane. UI test: terminal + tasks side by side, keys only in the focused pane, a press focusing the other, next pane, close (never the last). 234 app tests; full check passes.

Phase D built: the panes are remembered (app.toml panes: the split, each pane's view or placeholder and list/board, the focused one), restored when they hold together, a view remembered twice showing once. Terminals the VS Code way: Cmd-T starts another (from elsewhere it opens the terminals), a list at the terminal's right names each while there are several (the shell's window title, else the shell's name), a click shows one with the keys, its x kills it (never the last), a shell that exits leaves the list while others remain. Palette: Split pane right / down, Close pane and Next pane (with several), New terminal. The shortcuts sheet has a Panes section. Tests: restore round trip; UI for Cmd-T, the list, showing and killing. 236 app tests; full check passes.

review: 3 refuted, verified with probe tests that were then reverted. (1) model.rs:853 select_project calls enter_activity on the focused pane only, and enter_activity (activity.rs:28) refreshes activity_seen_before only when that pane is Activity. So with Activity in an unfocused pane, a project switch keeps the old project's mark: the new project's unseen Claude events show 0 new (expected all). (2) The Close/Esc order (ui/mod.rs:6277) checks reader.finding before the panel. With a Docs pane's find bar open, focusing another pane hides the bar (only the focused pane draws it), but Esc there with the panel open shuts the hidden bar and leaves the panel open. Partly pre-existing (leaving Docs by the sidebar), but panes make it the usual path. (3) A placeholder pane keeps view Inbox, so dock() (ui/mod.rs:2988) draws the Inbox filter button on it, and that filter changes the Inbox's shared display. Minor: select_project clears band/leaving on the focused pane only (model.rs:848-851). Restore does not check split shares or splits with fewer than 2 parts (hand-edited files only). Checked and clean: kill index math, exited pruning, act_on restored in pane_box and processors, clicks on unfocused rows (the capture focuses first), Split::remove renormalising.

Review fixes (all three REFUTED points, and the two minor): switching project starts every pane afresh (selection, band, fading rows) and the feed, wherever it shows, marks what is new since its own last visit; Esc closes the docs' find bar only while the Docs pane is focused, else it closes the panel as it should; a placeholder has no dock; restored panes must split into two parts or more with real shares. Regression tests for the feed in an unfocused pane and the placeholder's dock. 237 app tests; full check passes.

Changed with the developer (2026-10-19): a view the split does not have no longer replaces the focused pane. It shows alone over the split, which is kept as it was; picking a view the split has (sidebar, G keys, palette) brings the split back on that pane, as do the next pane's key and closing the view alone. Splitting a view shown alone takes it into the split beside where it was left; a placeholder still takes the view asked for. A view alone is not remembered as part of the split. docs/design.md now has a Panes section. Model test for the whole round; the UI test checks the docs alone and the terminal bringing the split back. 239 app tests; full check passes.

Changed with the developer (2026-10-19): while there is a split, its views sit grouped at the sidebar's top (a Split group, rows sliding in as they join, in the split's order, the focused pane lit, an empty pane as Empty pane) and leave their usual place; a click focuses the pane, a row's unsplit button (on hover) closes that pane, the focus staying where it was, and puts the view back in its place. Unsplitting to one pane under a view shown alone makes that view the one view. Model test for unsplit; the UI test now picks the terminal from the group and unsplits the tasks from it. 240 app tests; full check passes.
The split's group sits under the inbox and the feed, above Views (the developer's call, 2026-10-19).
The split's group back at the sidebar's top (the developer's call, 2026-10-19).

The dividers between panes are edges as the sidebar's (the developer's call, 2026-10-19): the glow following the pointer with the handle on it, brighter while dragged, no cursor change, a double-click evening the two panes out; dragged through the same window-wide drag as the sidebar's. UI test for the handle, the drag and the double-click. 240 app tests; full check passes.

Panes animate (the developer's call, 2026-10-19): a pane split off grows from nothing to its share as its neighbour gives way, fading in; a pane closed (its key, the placeholder's button, unsplit in the sidebar) shrinks away in the layout it left, drawn empty, fading out, before the rest take its room. The same timings as the panel's slide; none with less motion asked for. 240 app tests; full check passes.

The collapsed sidebar's rail groups the split's views too (the developer's call, 2026-10-19): a box at its top, the focused pane's button lit, the views out of their usual places; a click focuses the pane, a × at a button's corner (on hover) unsplits it. UI test. 241 app tests; full check passes.

Sidebar moves (the developer's call, 2026-10-19): a view joining the split slides from its place in the list up into the split's group, one leaving slides back down to its place, and the lines between slide to make room (on the rail too); a new placeholder fades in. Worked out from where each line sits in the two layouts, so a line starts exactly where it was. UI test: the row starts at its old place and ends in the group, and back on unsplit. 242 app tests; full check passes.

Plan (Claude), 2026-10-19. For the developer's ack. A research task: the deliverable is a doc, docs/research/tracking.md (it shows in the Docs view, linked to this task), and follow-up tasks proposed from it, nothing built.
1. Survey, from the tools' own docs and from how teams write about using them: Linear (teams, cycles, projects, milestones, initiatives, triage, project updates), Shape Up (six-week cycles, bets, appetite, hill charts, cool-down), Jira / Scrum (epics, sprints, story points), GitHub Projects (milestones, iterations, roadmaps), and briefly Height, Asana goals and Plane. For each: what the concept is for, how teams of 1-5, 10-50 and 100+ actually use it, where it helps, and where teams say it turns into ceremony or overhead.
2. What makes progress observable in practice: cycle burn-up, project status updates, hill charts, milestones, target dates; which ones teams keep using, and which they drop.
3. What changes with agents doing much of the work: Claude starts and finishes tasks, so delivery is fast and continuous. Which concepts still earn their place (outcomes, time boxes, review gates), and which only measured human throughput.
4. A recommendation for livtk: the smallest set of concepts above the task (likely one level of grouping with an outcome and an optional target, plus a time box only if it pays), how each maps onto livtk's model (nodes, the parent link, states, the human gates), how it reads in the app's grammar (a view, the panel, the graph), and how it scales from one developer to a large team without adding concepts. Each choice with its reason and what was left out, and why.
5. Proposed follow-up tasks (backlog) for whatever the developer accepts.
Sources cited inline. Research by web search and reading, in parallel where it helps; written so it can be read in ten minutes.

data.title: Detail opens three ways: side peek, center peek, full page
data.body:
The detail panel (a task's, a doc's) is fixed to the right. Make the way it opens a choice, as Notion's peek does. Asked by the developer (2026-10-19).

Notion, for reference: a page opened from a database opens one of three ways, set per database ("Open pages in") and switchable from the peek's own top bar.
- Side peek: the page in a panel at the right, the database still there beside it.
- Center peek: the page in a large modal over the dimmed database; Esc or a click outside closes it.
- Full page: the page in the database's place; back returns to the database.
The peek's bar carries: a button that switches between the three (a small menu, the current one ticked), "open as full page", and close. The choice sticks: the next page opens the same way.

For livtk
- The detail's bar gets a second button beside the close one: a menu of Side peek / Center peek / Full page, the current one ticked (and its key).
- Side peek: as now, the panel at the right.
- Center peek: the same detail in a centred modal over the window, as wide as reading wants (about 760px), dim behind; Esc or a click outside closes; the list behind keeps its selection.
- Full page: the detail in the pane that opened it (the tasks pane shows the task, behind the 46px bar), Esc or back gives the list back, the panel stays closed. In a split, only that pane.
- The choice is remembered across restarts and applies to every node's detail (the doc's details follow it too: side and center; a doc read is already full page).
- The detail's content becomes one piece used in all three places, not three copies.
- Tests: opening in each mode, switching from the bar, Esc in each, keys going where they should (the note field, the list behind), the choice remembered.

data.text: Plan (Claude), 2026-10-19. For the developer's ack. Model: a DetailMode (side, center, full) kept and saved with the window. UI: detail_panel's content split from its frame, so the same body renders as the right panel (as now, sliding), as a centred modal (the app's modal frame, dim behind, Esc and outside click close, the note field keeping its keys), and as full page inside the focused pane in the list's place (behind the 46px bar it already has; Esc gives the list back, the right panel closed meanwhile). The bar's new button opens a small menu of the three, the current ticked; picking one moves the open detail there at once. Docs' panel follows side/center. Steps: model + saved; content/frame split with no visible change; center peek; full page; the menu; tests (model: mode kept and restored; UI: each mode opens where it should, switching moves it, Esc in each, keys in the note field and in the list behind, a split pane's full page only in that pane).

Built: a DetailMode (side, center, full), remembered in app.toml. The detail's bar has a button beside its close: its icon the way it is open, a menu of Side peek / Center peek / Full page with the current ticked; picking one moves the open detail there at once, and the next opens the same way. Side peek: the panel as before. Center peek: the same detail in a card (760px, the window's height less a margin) over the dimmed window; the list behind keeps the keys (J and K move on and the detail follows, Esc closes), a press outside closes it. Full page: the detail in the list's place in the pane it was opened from (in a split, only there, whichever pane is focused), with its own keys (Esc closes; its note field types freely, outside the list's keys); no panel beside. The close button reads as a dock in side peek, a cross otherwise. A doc's details stay a side panel (a doc read is already the whole pane). One detail_panel framed three ways. Tests: each way, switching from the menu, Esc and a press outside, the detail following J, the choice sticking and surviving a restart, a full page in a split staying in its pane. 245 app tests; full check passes.
A full page hides the list's dock while the detail is open (the developer's call, 2026-10-19); Esc brings both back. In the UI test.

review: REFUTED. (1) Full page Esc skips the open menu: peek.rs:184 full_page Close handler calls close_detail without checking self.menu (NAV's handler at mod.rs:6340 closes a menu first). Open the detail-mode menu in full page, press Esc: the detail closes, self.menu stays Some(DetailMode), and the menu pops open again on the next Enter (probed). (2) detail_pane is never cleared or re-pointed (model.rs:1329 sets it only when detail opens afresh), and close_pane/unsplit leave detail open. Split tasks|inbox, full page in tasks, Cmd-Alt-W: the detail stays open but shows nowhere (panel_open is false; full_page wants a pane that no longer exists). In the inbox, 4 then changed the hidden LIV-1's priority 3->4 because acted_on prefers the open detail (probed); A/X act on it the same way, and only Esc gets rid of it. Related: with full page in pane A, Enter or J in pane B loads B's node into A's page. Existing detail/full_page/saved tests pass; probes reverted.

Review fixes (both REFUTED points, and the related one): Esc in a full page shuts a menu opened from it before the page; a full page goes with its pane (closed, unsplit, a view shown alone put away), so no detail stays open unseen for keys to act on; a detail opens in the pane it is opened from, and a full page no longer follows another pane's selection. A doc's details stay a side panel by choice (a doc read is the whole pane already). Model and UI regression tests. 246 app tests; full check passes.

data.title: Let a project switch off the parts of livtk's hooks it already covers
data.body:
## Why this is a task

Found by migrating a real repository onto livtk (the Nairos monorepo, 2026-10-19). That repo had
its own agent OS: 21 hooks of its own, including a SessionStart hook that injects branch and
service context, and a UserPromptSubmit hook that recalls its memory and nudges lessons.

Installing the livtk plugin did not fail. It made both run. Claude Code allows several hooks per
event, so nothing errored - the model simply received two overlapping blocks of context at session
start and before every prompt. Duplicated CONTEXT is worse than a crash, because nothing tells you.

The overlap was PARTIAL, which is the point. livtk's session-start emits a pointer to the CLI, the
skills, the tasks in progress, the gate list, and a paragraph of working protocol. For that project
the protocol paragraph duplicated its CLAUDE.md, which livtk cannot see and should not try to. The
tasks and the gates were exactly what it wanted. There is no way to keep two and drop the rest, so
the project kept its own hooks and ran both systems at once - which is how a tool meant to replace
an agent OS ends up running beside one.

Any project with established conventions will hit this. It is the first thing that makes livtk hard
to adopt where it is most useful.

## Goal

A project can tell livtk to stay quiet about what it already covers, and a project that wants one
hook per event has a documented way to get it.

## Approach

Two independent halves; the second is nearly free.

**1. Opt-out in `.livtk/config.toml`, at two levels.**

    [hooks]
    disable = ["session-start"]              # the whole hook
    [session_start]
    include = ["tasks", "gates"]             # or only these sections

Section names are what the reader sees, not internals: `intro` (the CLI and skills pointer),
`tasks` (in progress), `gates` (the human-only moves), `protocol` (how to work), `rules` (standing
lessons). For `user-prompt-submit`: `memory` (the recalled nodes) and `nudge` (the lesson prompt).
An unknown section name is an error at startup, not silence, so a typo cannot quietly turn
something off.

Default when the file says nothing: everything on, exactly as today. No existing project changes
behaviour.

**2. Document the plugin-free path, which already works.**

`livtk hook session-start` reads the hook JSON on stdin and writes Claude's own
`hookSpecificOutput` shape. So a project can call it from inside its OWN hook and merge the output -
one hook per event, no duplication. That works today and is in no document, so every project that
hits the collision believes its only options are everything or nothing.

Add a README section: install the plugin in a project with no hooks of its own; call `livtk hook`
from your own hook when you have them. Show the few lines that merge the two.

## Files

- wherever hook output is composed (`crates/livtk-cli/src/hook.rs` and its helpers)
- the config type that reads `.livtk/config.toml`
- `README.md`: the two installation shapes

## Acceptance check

- With `disable = ["session-start"]`, `livtk hook session-start` emits no `additionalContext`, and
  the other hooks are unaffected.
- With `include = ["tasks", "gates"]`, the output holds the in-progress list and the gate list and
  does NOT hold the protocol paragraph.
- An unknown section name fails at startup with a message naming it.
- A project with neither block sees byte-identical output to today.
- The README's merge example, pasted into a project's own SessionStart hook, produces one combined
  block.

data.title: Let a project declare its own kinds and relations, with today's set as the default
data.body:
## Why this is a task

From migrating the Nairos monorepo onto livtk, 2026-10-19. Its memory held seven kinds of thing and
eight kinds of link. livtk has four kinds (task, lesson, decision, finding) and five relations
(depends_on, relates, supersedes, learned_from, parent).

So the import lost meaning, quietly and permanently:
- `pattern` (2 nodes), `principle` (1), `contract` (1) and `service` (2) all became findings.
- `implements` (3 edges), `refines` (2), `amends` (2), `extends` (1) and `grounded-in` (1) all
  became `relates`.

Nothing broke. But "X implements Y" and "X is vaguely related to Y" are not the same sentence, and
after the import you cannot tell which one the author wrote.

The scaling problem is livtk's, not that project's. The next project arrives with its own
vocabulary, and there are two paths: it loses its words, or a kind gets added to livtk for it. Do
that a few times and livtk carries every user's nouns forever, with a state machine per noun to
maintain.

## Goal

A project declares the kinds and relations it needs. livtk keeps one engine. A project that
declares nothing gets exactly what it gets today.

## Approach

**The default is the current set, shipped as config rather than as code.** This is the part that
makes it safe: the four kinds and five relations become the built-in default table, expressed in
the same form a project would write. A project with no declaration sees no change at all, and the
default is also the worked example of the syntax.

    [[kinds]]
    name   = "incident"
    states = ["open", "mitigated", "closed"]
    start  = "open"
    human  = ["mitigated -> closed"]     # moves only the human may make
    key    = "INC"                        # key prefix

    [[relations]]
    name    = "implements"
    inverse = "implemented_by"            # optional, for the reverse view

What has to hold for a declared kind to be a first-class citizen rather than a second-class one:
- `livtk list --kind incident` works, and the app's sidebar shows it.
- its states appear in the detail panel's state flow and on the board as columns.
- `[gates] human` entries can name it (`incident: mitigated -> closed`).
- search and recall include it.
- a kind cannot be removed from config while nodes of it exist - that would orphan them - so
  removal needs an explicit migration command or a refusal that says which nodes block it.

Relations are simpler: a name, an optional inverse for display, and the cycle rule staying with
`depends_on` alone.

## Files

- the config type and its defaults (the built-in table moves there)
- the kind and state enums, which become data rather than Rust variants
- `crates/livtk-core/src/store.rs`: the transition and gate checks read the table
- the app: sidebar, board columns, the detail panel's state flow
- `README.md`

## Acceptance check

- A project with no `[[kinds]]` or `[[relations]]` behaves identically to the current release:
  same kinds, same keys, same states, same gates. Prove it against an existing project's log by
  rebuilding and comparing the rows.
- A declared `incident` kind can be created, listed, moved through its states, gated for the human,
  found by search, and seen in the app with its own band and columns.
- A declared `implements` relation is addable, removable, shown in the detail panel, and the
  reverse view uses its inverse.
- Removing a kind from config while nodes of it exist is refused, and the message names them.

data.title: Take formatting and build-checking out of livtk, and keep only the parts livtk uniquely knows
data.body:
## Why this is a task

From migrating the Nairos monorepo onto livtk, 2026-10-19, and the developer's own verdict on the
feature: the built-in `[hooks] format` and `[hooks] check` commands are not worth keeping.

The evidence from that migration is that neither could do the job, so the project kept its own
hooks and ran them beside livtk's - the same collision as TAS-53, wearing different clothes:

`format` takes ONE command over an extension list. That project's formatter needed three things the
field cannot express: skip generated directories (`node_modules`, `dist`, `.next`, generated,
`.turbo`, `coverage`); refuse files OUTSIDE the project, because that session edits three
repositories and prettier otherwise resolves a different repo's config and rewrites unrelated
lines; and run `eslint --fix` before `prettier`, two tools in order.

`check` takes ONE fixed command. That project's check works out which applications actually changed
and only typechecks those, exits 2 so the agent is blocked with the errors in front of it, and
skips quietly when a worktree has no dependencies installed. A single command cannot scope, cannot
degrade, and has no documented way to return its failure text.

The deeper point, and the reason this is a removal rather than an extension: FORMATTING A FILE AND
RUNNING A BUILD ARE NOT LIVTK'S BUSINESS. livtk is tasks and memory. A formatter inside it is scope
creep that then collides with every project that already formats - and every project does.

## Goal

livtk stops running other people's commands. The two hook points it keeps are the ones only livtk
can answer, because they are about plans and tasks.

## Approach

**Remove** `[hooks] format`, `format_extensions`, `check` and `check_agents`, and the PostToolUse
and SubagentStop registrations that exist to run them. A project that wants formatting writes a
PostToolUse hook; that is what the mechanism is for, every project already has an opinion, and
Claude Code's own documentation covers it. Deprecate for one release with a warning naming the
replacement, then delete - and say in the README where formatting went, so the removal is not read
as an oversight.

**Keep, and make the point of those hooks:** what livtk alone knows. A SubagentStop hook has a real
livtk-shaped job - refusing a stop that leaves the project inconsistent:
- a task is still `doing` and its plan changed since it was acknowledged (see TAS-57);
- a task is `doing` with no note at all, so nothing was recorded about what was tried;
- the agent is stopping with an acknowledged task half-moved.

Those are refusals livtk can justify and no project can write for itself. That is the right
replacement for "run my command": enforce my domain.

The same reasoning applies to PostToolUse. If livtk has nothing of its own to do there, it should
not register the hook at all; an event with a hook that does nothing is a thing to explain forever.

## Files

- the config type: remove the four fields
- `crates/livtk-cli/src/hook.rs`: drop the command runners, add the consistency refusals
- `plugin/hooks/hooks.json`: drop PostToolUse if nothing remains for it
- `README.md`: the removal, where formatting goes instead, and what SubagentStop now refuses

## Acceptance check

- A config still carrying `format` or `check` loads with a warning that names the replacement, for
  one release; after that it is an error.
- No `livtk` process starts a formatter or a build any more: grep the crates for the runner and it
  is gone.
- An agent that tries to stop while a task is `doing` with a plan edited after its acknowledgement
  is refused, and the message says which task and why.
- An agent that stops with a clean board is not refused.
- A project that formats with its own PostToolUse hook is unaffected either way.

data.title: Make livtk readable by machines, and give a local developer an optional markdown mirror
data.body:
## Why this is a task

Two halves of one problem, found while verifying an import of 139 tasks and 139 memory nodes into
livtk (Nairos monorepo, 2026-10-19).

**Half one: the JSON is too thin to automate over.** `livtk list --kind task --all --json` returns
id, key, kind, title, state, priority, updated, blocked, standing and parent - and no `props`, no
`body`. The importer had written a `board_id` prop on every task precisely so the verification
could match old to new; it could not be read back. The check had to match on node ids instead,
which happened to work only because that importer had reused the old uuids as node ids. Every
project automating over livtk will hit this and write its own workaround.

**Half two: the work stopped being greppable, and that is not simply a loss to accept.** With the
board in the event log, `grep -r` over 139 task bodies is gone and a task no longer appears in a
pull request diff. But the right answer is NOT to put the truth back into files: the developer's
direction is explicit - tasks will not stay locally managed, a team's tasks will live on a server,
and a file-per-task model would be exactly the wrong thing to design around now. What IS needed is
an option for a developer running locally, who wants to grep and diff their own project. Both
things, not one at the expense of the other.

## Goal

Anything a project wants to automate over livtk can be read from its JSON. A developer who wants
their work on disk as markdown can have it, as a DERIVED copy that is never the source of truth.

## Approach

**JSON.** Add `props` and `body` to the row, or - better, since bodies are large and most callers
do not want them - a `--fields` flag: `livtk list --json --fields key,state,props`. `livtk show
--json` should return the whole node including props, body, links and notes, because that is the
call that means "give me everything about this one". Keep today's default row shape so nothing
breaks.

**The mirror.** `livtk export --dir .livtk/export` writes one markdown file per node: frontmatter
for the fields, the body underneath, links listed. It is regenerated, never read back, and the
documentation says so in the same breath as announcing it - because the moment someone edits an
exported file and expects it to matter, the event log has a rival. Suggested defaults: the
directory is gitignored, and `export --check` exits non-zero if it is stale, so a project that
wants it in git can gate that in CI.

**Design it for the server that is coming.** Export is a client-side projection of whatever the
client can see. When the team model arrives and the log lives on a server, `export` still means
"write what I can read to disk", and nothing about it assumes local files are the truth. That is
the whole reason it is an export command rather than a storage mode.

## Files

- `crates/livtk-cli/src/output.rs` and the list and show commands: `--fields`, props, body
- a new `export` command in the CLI, reading the projection
- `README.md`: the JSON surface, and export with its "derived, never authoritative" warning

## Acceptance check

- `livtk list --json --fields key,props` returns props for every row, and the default `--json`
  output is unchanged from today.
- `livtk show KEY --json` returns body, props, links and notes in one object.
- `livtk export --dir X` writes one file per node; `grep -r` over X finds a phrase that exists only
  in a task body; a second run with no changes rewrites nothing.
- `livtk export --check` exits non-zero after a task changes and zero once re-exported.
- Editing an exported file changes nothing in livtk, and the README says that where a reader will
  see it before trying.

data.title: Close the acknowledgement hole: a plan edited while in progress keeps the human's approval
data.body:
## Why this is a task

Found while using livtk to migrate a repository onto livtk, 2026-10-19, and already recorded as a
finding in that project.

The rule is that changing the title or body of an ACKED task sends it back to `planned`, so the
human acknowledges the plan again. A task already in `doing` keeps its state when its body changes.

That hole was hit on the first real task. The plan for an import said 133 tasks, 132 memory nodes
and 122 lessons. Measuring found 139 tasks, found that the lesson journal held 122 LINES but 60
lessons, and found that importing both the ratified lessons and the convention nodes would have put
every rule in twice. The plan was rewritten to match - a materially different plan, with different
numbers and a different memory model - and it carried the human's acknowledgement with it, silently,
because the task was `doing` by then.

It only went back for a second acknowledgement because the agent chose to say so and moved it
`doing -> acked -> planned` by hand. A gate whose integrity depends on the agent volunteering is
the one thing the gate exists not to depend on.

## Goal

A plan that changes materially after it was acknowledged cannot keep that acknowledgement, whatever
state the task is in.

## Approach

Interrupting work for a typo would be worse than the hole, so this is not "bounce on every edit".
Two shapes, and the second is probably right:

**A. Bounce `doing` to `planned` as well**, but only on a material change - a body edit beyond some
threshold, or any edit to a section the plan skill names (Goal, Approach, Acceptance check), while
leaving title case and whitespace alone. Simple, and it stops the work, which is honest but
blunt.

**B. Mark the task as carrying an unacknowledged plan, and let the work continue.** A flag on the
node, set when an acked-or-later task's body changes, cleared by a fresh `livtk ack`. The task
stays `doing`; the inbox shows it; the app marks it; and - the part that gives it teeth - the
SubagentStop refusal from TAS-55 and `livtk done` refuse while the flag is set. Nothing is
interrupted, nothing is finished on an approval that no longer matches what was built.

B is recommended: it matches why the rule exists (the human approves what gets built, not what gets
started) without making every clarification a stop-the-line.

Either way the event log needs it to be visible after the fact: a reader should be able to see that
a plan changed after approval and when it was approved again.

## Files

- `crates/livtk-core/src/store.rs`: the set path for title and body, the flag, and the refusals
- the inbox query
- the app: the badge or marker, and the acknowledge action clearing it
- `README.md`: the rule, stated for every state rather than only for `acked`

## Acceptance check

- Editing the body of a `doing` task sets the flag; `livtk show` and `livtk inbox` both say so.
- `livtk done` on that task is refused with a message naming the unacknowledged plan; after
  `livtk ack` it succeeds.
- A whitespace-only or title-case edit does not set the flag.
- The log shows the change and the later acknowledgement as separate events, so the sequence is
  readable afterwards.
- An `acked` task still goes back to `planned` on a body edit, as it does today.

data.text: Built: docs/research/tracking.md (linked), from three parallel research briefs (Linear; Shape Up, Scrum/Jira, GitHub, Asana, Plane, Kanban and the evidence; planning when agents do the work). Recommendation: keep the task as the unit and add one concept above it, the project (an outcome with a Done when, optional target and owner; proposed -> active is a human gate; tasks join by parent; projects nest, covering milestones and initiatives), with computed progress, a 'waiting on you' count per human gate, written health updates by Claude (stale after a week), and a nudge past three active. Left out, with reasons: cycles, estimates, separate initiative/milestone/epic kinds, separate triage, appetite as time. Four follow-up tasks proposed in the doc (core and CLI; the app; Claude's skills; flow numbers), to be created once the developer accepts what they want.

data.title: Settings as a view: personal and project settings in one place
data.body:
Asked by the developer (2026-10-19): a Settings entry under the shortcuts hint in the sidebar, opening settings the way claude.ai and other modern apps do; the place where what TAS-53, 54, 55 and 56 make configurable is set without editing TOML by hand.

The shape (as claude.ai, Linear, Raycast): settings take the window's middle as a view of their own, a list of sections at their left and the section's settings at the right, Esc or the sidebar leaving them. Not a modal: there will be enough of them to need room, and a view can be split beside the work like any other.

Two kinds of settings, kept apart because they live in different places and belong to different people:
- **You** (the app's own, kept in app.toml, private): Appearance (reading size and density, motion), Detail (how a task opens: side, center, full), Panes and terminal (the terminal's shell and font size), Updates (check now, the build installed and its notes), Shortcuts (the sheet, read-only for now).
- **This project** (.livtk/config.toml, committed, shared with the team): General (the key prefix, the docs folder), Claude (what livtk tells Claude at session start and before each prompt, section by section: TAS-53's switches), Kinds and relations (the built-in set and the project's own: TAS-54), Gates (the moves only the human may make), Export (the markdown mirror: TAS-56).
Each project setting says it is committed and shared; each personal one that it is only yours.

Rules: every setting shows its default and whether it differs; a project setting is written through the core, validated (an unknown section, a kind still in use), never as raw text; nothing here that a person would not change.

The old Settings modal (Cmd-,) opens this view instead. Tests: each section reads and writes its setting; project settings round-trip through config.toml and the CLI sees them; an invalid value is refused with its reason.

data.text: Plan (Claude), 2026-10-19. For the developer's ack. Built after TAS-53, 54, 55 and 56, so each project section edits something real; until then those sections are not shown. Steps: a Settings view (View::Settings, not in the sidebar's views list but its own row under Shortcuts, Cmd-, too), its left list of sections grouped You / This project; the personal sections over app.toml (moving the Settings modal's reading options and the detail mode there); the project sections over a core API that reads and writes config.toml with validation (no hand-written TOML), one per feature as it lands; tests per section.

Built, shape B: a real change (spacing and case aside) to the title or body of a task already doing or in review marks it 'replanned' (a prop, so the log shows the change and the later acknowledgement as their own events). The work goes on; the task waits in the inbox ('ack the changed plan'), livtk show says 'plan changed since acknowledged', the app tags its row Plan changed and its panel says so with an Acknowledge button (A works too). Done is refused while marked, naming the task and the way out. livtk ack (a new core Ack command) clears the mark for the human (Claude refused) and keeps the state; on a planned task it acknowledges as before. Sent back to planned or backlog, the mark goes. An acked task still goes back to planned on an edit. Tests: core (spacing/case, mark, inbox, done refused, Claude refused, ack clears, log events, acked->planned unchanged), app (inbox, A acknowledges, work goes on). README states the rule for every state. Full check passes.

## Goal

A plan that changes materially after it was acknowledged cannot keep that acknowledgement, whatever
state the task is in.

## Approach

Interrupting work for a typo would be worse than the hole, so this is not "bounce on every edit".
Two shapes, and the second is probably right:

**A. Bounce `doing` to `planned` as well**, but only on a material change - a body edit beyond some
threshold, or any edit to a section the plan skill names (Goal, Approach, Acceptance check), while
leaving title case and whitespace alone. Simple, and it stops the work, which is honest but
blunt.

**B. Mark the task as carrying an unacknowledged plan, and let the work continue.** A flag on the
node, set when an acked-or-later task's body changes, cleared by a fresh `livtk ack`. The task
stays `doing`; the inbox shows it; the app marks it; and - the part that gives it teeth - the
SubagentStop refusal from TAS-55 and `livtk done` refuse while the flag is set. Nothing is
interrupted, nothing is finished on an approval that no longer matches what was built.

B is recommended: it matches why the rule exists (the human approves what gets built, not what gets
started) without making every clarification a stop-the-line.

Either way the event log needs it to be visible after the fact: a reader should be able to see that
a plan changed after approval and when it was approved again.

## Files

- `crates/livtk-core/src/store.rs`: the set path for title and body, the flag, and the refusals
- the inbox query
- the app: the badge or marker, and the acknowledge action clearing it
- `README.md`: the rule, stated for every state rather than only for `acked`

## Acceptance check

- Editing the body of a `doing` task sets the flag; `livtk show` and `livtk inbox` both say so.
- `livtk done` on that task is refused with a message naming the unacknowledged plan; after
  `livtk ack` it succeeds.
- A whitespace-only or title-case edit does not set the flag.
- The log shows the change and the later acknowledgement as separate events, so the sequence is
  readable afterwards.
- An `acked` task still goes back to `planned` on a body edit, as it does today.

data.title: Fix the declared kinds bugs the TAS-54 review found
data.body:
Follow-up to TAS-54 (done). Its refuter note on TAS-54 has the probes; this task fixes them.

## Bugs

1. **One registry for every project in a process.** `REGISTRY` in `crates/livtk-core/src/model.rs` is global; `declare_kinds` keeps the newest declaration. With two projects open in the app (A: `incident{open,closed}` key INC, B: `incident{new,triaged,resolved}` key OPS), A's create writes `OPS-1` in state `new` into A's log. Also: `validate_project_prefix` checks `Kind::all()` across projects (a project with prefix OPS fails to open); a project that declares nothing accepts other projects' kinds; `check_kinds` passes on kinds only another project declares.
2. **Closed/active ignore the kind.** `State::is_closed`/`is_active` use built-in rules for built-in state names, and a declared state counts as closed for every kind if any kind closes it. `bug{open,done,verified}`: BUG-1 in `done` is hidden from list. `rfc{draft,accepted}`: RFC-1 in `accepted` (its closed state) still shows as active. `pattern{draft,closed,archived}` with closed=[archived]: PAT-1 in `closed` is hidden.
3. **"A used kind cannot leave the config" only holds while livtk.db exists.** `check_kinds` (workspace.rs) runs after `catch_up` and reads only the store. With a fresh db, the dropped kind's `node.create` is skipped as Garbage ("unknown kind") with only warnings and exit 0, so the node and its links vanish. A dropped state is not guarded: with the db, every command fails "unknown state mitigated" without naming the node; with a fresh db the move is silently lost. Dropping a built-in-named state leaves the node in a state its kind no longer has.
4. Minor: `--json show` leaves out declared relations; the unknown-state error (State FromStr) lists only built-in states; a bad `--kind` exits 1 where clap gave 2.

## Plan

- (2) Add `Kind::is_closed(state)`, `is_active(state)`, `is_dismissed(state)`: a declared kind uses its own `closed` list and has no dismissed states; a built-in kind uses the State rules. Make `State::is_closed`/`is_active` built-in only. **Already started, uncommitted in `crates/livtk-core/src/model.rs` (`git diff`)**. Then switch the call sites where the kind is known: livtk-app `model.rs` ~2082, 2217, 2282, 2354; `ui/mod.rs` 2908, 4684, 4873, 7109; `palette.rs` 476, 520; `theme.rs` 109, 145; `saved.rs` 296; `graph.rs` 540; livtk-cli `main.rs` ~552 (List filter) and `output.rs` 142; core `workspace.rs` ~1533 and `signal.rs` 196, 221, 284, 292.
- (1) Record the owner (the project folder) on each `KindDef` and declared relation. `declare_kinds(owner, specs)` / `declare_relations(owner, specs)` refuse a different declaration of the same name by another open project, with an error naming that project. In `parse_config`, pass the owner. `check_kinds` accepts only built-in kinds and the project's own `config.kinds`. `validate_project_prefix` checks only the project's own keys.
- (3) Run `check_kinds` *before* `catch_up` when the store is current. Also check each node's state belongs to its kind (a new `Store::states_in_use()` -> (kind, state, min key)) and name the node. When parsing the log, an unknown kind, state or relation in an event of the current format version is a hard config error naming the node (not Garbage). Older-format garbage stays a warning.
- (4) Put declared relations in `--json show`; list declared states in the unknown-state error; make a bad `--kind` exit 2.

## Acceptance check

- Two projects open in one process that declare the same kind name differently: the second is refused with a message naming the first; neither log gains the other's keys or states. A project that declares nothing rejects other projects' kinds.
- `bug{open,done,verified}`: BUG-1 in `done` shows in `list`; `rfc{draft,accepted}`: RFC-1 in `accepted` is hidden without `--all`; `pattern` with closed=[archived]: PAT-1 in `closed` shows.
- Removing a used kind or state from config is refused, naming the nodes, both with the existing db and after deleting livtk.db.
- The TAS-54 proof still holds: with no declarations, rebuilt rows are byte-identical to the previous release for every built-in kind.
- Tests for each of the above; `scripts/check` passes.

data.text: Bugs found in review are tracked in TAS-59.

A git stash I ran to benchmark the previous commit took .livtk/events.jsonl with it for a minute; the app showed TAS-59 as planned and the human acked it again. Restored: every event kept, the second ack after the first; back to doing.

Fixed. (1) Each declared kind and relation records its project; another open project declaring the same name differently is refused, naming the first. A project creates only its own kinds (Workspace::owns); check_kinds accepts only built-ins and its own [[kinds]]; the project prefix is checked against built-in keys only. (2) Kind::is_closed/is_active/is_dismissed: a declared kind closes only at its own closed states, has no dismissed ones; State's are built-in only. Used everywhere the kind is known: CLI list and blocked flag, start-blocked check, signals, app filters, board columns, marks, colours, graph, palette, saved views (Brief carries its kind, not in JSON). (3) On open the store's kinds and states are checked against the config before the log is read; a log line of this format naming an undeclared kind, state or relation stops livtk naming the node (from the store or its creation line), with or without livtk.db; a newer format's lines are still skipped. One index pass, so list on 10k tasks stays ~8ms. (4) --json show has a 'declared' object (to, from, inverse) only when relations are declared; unknown state lists declared ones; a bad --kind or state exits 2. Proof: this repo's log rebuilt with build 174 and this build gives byte-identical list/show/search output for every built-in kind. Tests: core two-projects; CLI closed-by-kind, dropped kind/state with and without db, show JSON + exit 2. scripts/check passes.

review: REFUTED (3) dropped state after deleting livtk.db: Workspace::open (crates/livtk-core/src/workspace.rs ~481-491) now runs check_kinds only when the store is current; the fresh-db branch runs catch_up and never checks. refuse_undeclared only catches names the registry does not know at all, so a dropped state that still parses is replayed silently. Repro: bug{open,done,verified}, BUG-1 -> done, config to bug{open,verified}, rm .livtk/livtk.db*: 'livtk list --kind bug --all' exits 0 and shows BUG-1 under DONE; only the next command refuses. Same for a dropped declared state another kind of the project still has (incident drops mitigated, ticket{new,mitigated} keeps it: INC-1 in mitigated, first fresh-db command exits 0). The CLI test only covers a state no kind still has. UPHELD (1) core test two_projects_in_one_process_keep_their_own_kinds passes; declare_kinds refuses naming the other owner; lower() Create checks owns(). UPHELD (2) CLI test passes for bug/rfc/pattern; Kind::is_closed/is_active use the declared closed list. UPHELD (4) rebuilt this repo's log with build 174 (ee16544) and this build: nodes and edges rows identical (947/13), --json list --all identical for task/lesson/decision/finding. UNVERIFIABLE (5) scripts/check not run, per review scope; the new tests pass, but none covers the case above.

Review fix: on a fresh livtk.db, open now also checks the built store's kinds and states after the catch-up, so a dropped state still known by name (built-in like done, or another kind's) is refused on the first command, naming the node. Test covers the reviewer's repro. scripts/check passes.

data.title: Settings: show or hide the state graph in a task's details
data.body:
## Goal

The state graph (the flow of a node's states, with the moves it can make) sits in the detail panel above the body. Some people want it, some want the room. A personal setting decides, as the detail mode does.

## Plan

- Model: a `show_state_flow: bool` (default on, as today), kept with the other personal settings in the saved file (`model/saved.rs`, beside `detail_mode`; absent means on, so existing saved files keep the graph).
- Settings › Opening work (`ui/settings.rs` `detail_section`): a second row, "State graph": "The states a task moves through, above its body." with an on/off switch (the switch the Appearance section uses, or a two-choice segmented control Show / Hide if there is none).
- Detail panel (`ui/mod.rs` ~5214): the graph shows when its kind has a flow *and* the setting is on, in every detail mode (side, centre, full page). Hidden, the panel loses nothing else: state can still be changed from the state menu.
- `docs/design.md`: one line under Settings.

## Acceptance check

- Settings › Opening work has a State graph switch; turning it off hides the graph in the detail panel at once, in side, centre and full page modes; on brings it back.
- The choice survives a restart; a saved file without it shows the graph.
- The state can still be changed with the graph hidden.
- An app test covers: off hides the flow element, on shows it, the saved value round-trips and defaults to on.

data.text: Built. Settings › Opening work has a State graph switch under 'Open a task as' (on by default). Off hides the graph in the detail at once, in side, centre and full page; the detail's own state menu stays, so nothing is lost. Kept with the personal settings (hide_state_flow in the app's saved file; absent means shown). design.md: such detail parts are personal switches, never per node. App test: default shown, the switch hides it in all three modes with the state menu kept, saved and restored, a file without it shows it. scripts/check passes.

review: UPHELD all four points. (1) Settings > Opening work row 'State graph' toggle (ui/settings.rs detail_section) flips model.hide_state_flow + cx.notify; the only flow render site (ui/mod.rs:5214) is gated on it, shared by side/centre/full; test asserts state-flow gone in all three and back on restore. (2) Saved.hide_state_flow written by saved(), read by restore(), persisted by the tick's persist() diff; Saved is #[serde(default)] so a file without the key gives false = shown. (3) detail-state menu (state_button) does not depend on the setting; test asserts it present in every mode while hidden. (4) cargo test -p livtk-app --test app the_state_graph: 1 passed. Minor, not refuting: the absent-key default is tested via Saved::default(), not by parsing a TOML missing the key; changing state while hidden is checked only by the menu being present, not by actually moving a state.
Closed both review gaps in the test: it now moves the task (acked from the detail's state menu) with the graph hidden, and restores from a real app.toml written without the key.
accepted, read the docs and it well aligns with the vision

data.title: Projects in the core and CLI: an outcome above tasks, with computed progress
data.body:
From TAS-26 (docs/research/tracking.md, "Recommendation for livtk"), accepted 2026-10-21.

## Goal
One concept above the task: the project, an outcome with a "Done when", so progress is observable without estimates.

## Plan
- A built-in kind `project` (key `PRJ`, fixed like LES/DEC/FND): states proposed -> active -> done, plus paused and dropped. proposed -> active and -> done are the human's moves (a gate, like ack). Claude may create (propose) one.
- Body holds the outcome, ending in a `Done when:` line; optional `target` (date) and `owner` (a human) as props.
- Tasks join by the existing `parent` link (one project per task); projects nest by the same link.
- Computed, never typed: done/total tasks (nested projects counted through), and waiting on you: how many of its tasks sit at each human gate (planned -> ack, review -> done) and the oldest wait.
- Health updates: a note with a flag (on_track, at_risk, off_track), what moved, what is next; `livtk project update KEY --health at_risk "..."`. An active project with none in 7 days reads "update missing".
- CLI: `livtk project new | list | show | update`; `livtk list` shows a task's project; `--json` everywhere. More than three active: `project list` says so.
- FORMAT_VERSION: a new kind in events -> bump with min_version as TAS-54 did; older livtk skips with the update warning.

## Acceptance check
- A project is created as proposed; Claude cannot activate or finish it, the human can.
- Tasks and sub-projects join by parent; `project show` gives done/total through nesting and the waiting-on-you counts with oldest wait, matching a hand count in a test.
- A health update is recorded and shown; a week without one reads "update missing" (tested with a fixed clock).
- A project with no projects declared changes nothing else: this repo's rows rebuilt are byte-identical for the other kinds.
- Tests in core and CLI; scripts/check passes.

data.title: Runs in the core and CLI: agents on tasks, headless sessions, the conversation as notes
data.body:
From TAS-65 (docs/research/agents.md, "The work" 2), shaped by the spike (TAS-66).

## Plan
- A task's `agent` prop (set by the human or accepted from the suggestion: plan from backlog, build when acked, review in review, a stage line in the agent's file).
- Run records on the task (started: session, agent, stage; ended: done, failed, stopped) as events; live state beside the log, not in it.
- A runner in the core that starts, resumes and stops a headless session for a task, in place or in a worktree.
- Needs you: a question or a permission becomes a note on the task flagged needs-you (the Inbox lists it); a note from the human on a task with a waiting run resumes it with that note; Claude's replies come back as notes.

- CLI: `livtk agent set KEY NAME`, `livtk run KEY`, `livtk runs`, `livtk run stop KEY`.
- The stop check for a session started as the implementer; `livtk` from a worktree writes to the main checkout's log.

## Acceptance check
- A run started on an acked task builds it; a question it asks shows as a needs-you note and in the Inbox; a reply note resumes it; stop ends it cleanly with the work kept. Tested against a stub `claude` that speaks the recorded stream-json.

- Tests in core and CLI; scripts/check passes.

data.title: The Agents place: watch Claude sessions, and create, edit and remove agents
data.body:
From TAS-65 (docs/research/agents.md, "In the app" and "Designing agents"). Moved first at the human's word on TAS-65 (2026-10-21): the views to monitor agents come before livtk starts runs itself, so this no longer waits for TAS-67.

## Goal
A place in the app to see every Claude session working in this project, and to make, change and remove the agents they can run as.

## Plan
- **Agents**, a sidebar place (after Docs), with two parts.
- **Sessions:** Claude Code's own list (`claude agents --json`: interactive and background sessions, with pid, folder, name, session id, started, and status busy / waiting / idle), read off the window's thread every few seconds while the place is open, kept to this project's folder and its worktrees.
  - Rows: name, state as people say it (Working, Needs you, Idle), interactive or background, how long it has run. Needs you first.
  - The panel: the session, and what livtk saw Claude do in this project since it started (the tasks it moved and noted, newest first).
  - Actions: Open (resume it in the app's terminal: `claude --resume <id>`), and Stop for a background session (`claude stop <id>`).
  - Without the `claude` command, the part says so and how to get it.
- **Agents:** the agent files, grouped livtk's (the plugin's, read-only), this project's (`.claude/agents/`), yours (`~/.claude/agents/`).
  - An agent's page: name, description, the tools it may use as switches, model, and its instructions in the docs editor.
  - New agent: blank, or a copy of any agent; you choose where it lives (this project or yours).
  - Remove: for this project's and yours, after a confirmation; livtk's own can only be copied.
  - Saving writes a valid Claude Code agent file (frontmatter + body); a bad name or a clash says why and writes nothing.
- docs/design.md: the Agents place, as the grammar's agentic views begin.

## Acceptance check
- With a stub `claude` that prints a recorded `agents --json`, the Sessions list shows this project's sessions only, Needs you first, and follows the stub as it changes; Stop calls `claude stop <id>` for a background session.
- An agent created in the app is a file Claude Code reads (name, description, tools, model, body), in the chosen place; editing changes it; removing deletes it after a confirmation; livtk's own cannot be edited or removed.
- App tests for both (behaviour only); scripts/check passes.

Saving an edit drops every other frontmatter key (color, permissionMode, skills, hooks, mcpServers). Worse, a YAML-list `tools:\n  - Read\n  - Grep` reads as no tools, and saving writes no tools line, so the agent gets every tool. A block description (`description: >`) reads as ">" and is saved as ">". Also: render() writes the description unquoted, so a description with ": " gives frontmatter that is not valid YAML. Whether Claude Code still loads such a file is untested. No app test edits an existing agent (the test only copies, saves and removes), so editing has no app test.
